stem: Current of 4.8 amperes is flowing through a conductor. The number of electrons per second will be
solution:
[PRINTED DEFECT] Two options carry the identical value \(7.68 \times 10^{21}\). Here the duplicate is a DISTRACTOR, not the answer, so the key is unaffected.

Given \(I = 4.8\,\text{A}\) and \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}\).
Charge passing in one second is \(q = It = 4.8\,\text{C}\), carried by \(n\) electrons, so \(n = \dfrac{I}{e}\).
\(n = \dfrac{4.8}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 3 \times 10^{19}\) electrons per second.
The value \(7.68 \times 10^{21}\) comes from multiplying by the electronic charge instead of dividing, which gives \(7.68 \times 10^{-19}\) and not a count at all.
Matches option A.
reviewNote: Printed defect already recorded in the note: options (b) and (c) are character-for-character identical, both \(7.68 \times 10^{21}\). It is a duplicated DISTRACTOR rather than a duplicated answer - the computed value \(3 \times 10^{19}\) sits on a different option and is unique to it - so no two options can both be correct and the OMR key is unaffected. Confirmed on the rendered page.

stem: The resistance of a wire of uniform diameter \(d\) and length \(L\) is \(R\). The resistance of another wire of the same material but diameter \(2d\) and length \(4L\) will be
solution:
\(R = \dfrac{\rho L}{A}\) with \(A = \dfrac{\pi d^{2}}{4}\), so \(R \propto \dfrac{L}{d^{2}}\).
\(\dfrac{R'}{R} = \dfrac{4L}{L} \times \left(\dfrac{d}{2d}\right)^{2} = 4 \times \dfrac{1}{4}\).
\(= 1\), so \(R' = R\).
The fourfold length and the fourfold area cancel exactly.
Matches option B.

stem: If the resistance of wire is is \(10\,\Omega\). Its length is increased by 10% by stretching. The new resistance will be
solution:
[PRINTED DEFECT] No printed option is correct. Stretching at constant volume raises the resistance by the square of the length ratio, giving 12.1 ohm, and that value is not offered. The nearest printed value is 13 ohm.

Stretching a wire conserves its volume, so \(AL\) is fixed and \(R = \dfrac{\rho L}{A} = \dfrac{\rho L^{2}}{AL} \propto L^{2}\).
\(L' = 1.1L\), so \(R' = R(1.1)^{2} = 10 \times 1.21\).
\(= 12.1\,\Omega\).
No printed value is \(12.1\,\Omega\); of the four, \(13\,\Omega\) lies nearest, \(0.9\) away against \(1.1\) for \(11\,\Omega\).
Matches option C.
reviewNote: NO PRINTED OPTION IS CORRECT. The true value is \(12.1\,\Omega\) (\(R \propto L^{2}\) at constant volume, so \(10 \times 1.21\)); the four printed values are \(10\), \(1.2\), \(13\) and \(11\,\Omega\). I keyed the nearest printed value, \(13\,\Omega\), purely so the OMR has a key. Two further facts for whoever adjudicates. (1) I re-read all four options on the page myself at 3x: (a) really is \(10\,\Omega\), not \(12\,\Omega\). That matters, because the standard printed form of this item is 12 / 1.2 / 13 / 11 with the key on \(12\,\Omega\), so the likeliest single-character corruption is that (a) should read \(12\,\Omega\) - the stem's own \(10\,\Omega\) appears to have been copied into it. (2) \(10\,\Omega\) is impossible on physical grounds anyway, since stretching can only increase resistance. \(11\,\Omega\) is the trap for the student who scales \(R\) by 10% instead of by \((1.1)^{2}\), so it is a distractor and not the intended key. If the source paper can be traced, (a) should be corrected to \(12\,\Omega\) and the key moved there; until then no answer is defensible on the paper as printed.

stem: The charge of an electron is \(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C. How many electrons strike the screen of a cathode ray tube each second when the beam current is 16 mA
solution:
Given \(I = 16\,\text{mA} = 16 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{A}\) and \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}\).
\(n = \dfrac{I}{e} = \dfrac{16 \times 10^{-3}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}}\).
\(= 10 \times 10^{16} = 10^{17}\) electrons per second.
A count of particles cannot be a negative power of ten, so the two fractional values are not candidates.
Matches option A.

stem: The resistance of a 5 cm long wire is \(10\,\Omega\). It is uniformly stretched so that its length becomes 20 cm. The resistance of the wire is
solution:
Stretching conserves volume, so \(R \propto L^{2}\).
\(\dfrac{L'}{L} = \dfrac{20}{5} = 4\).
\(R' = R \times 4^{2} = 10 \times 16\).
\(= 160\,\Omega\).
Matches option A.

stem: Find the total current flowing in circuit.
solution:
From the figure the \(5\,\Omega\) and the \(8\,\Omega\) are in parallel, that pair is in series with the second \(5\,\Omega\), and the whole of that upper branch is in parallel with the \(3\,\Omega\) across the \(12\,\text{V}\) cell.
\(5 \parallel 8 = \dfrac{5 \times 8}{5+8} = \dfrac{40}{13}\,\Omega\).
Upper branch \(= \dfrac{40}{13} + 5 = \dfrac{105}{13}\,\Omega\).
\(R_{eq} = \dfrac{\frac{105}{13} \times 3}{\frac{105}{13} + 3} = \dfrac{315}{144} = 2.1875\,\Omega\).
\(I = \dfrac{V}{R_{eq}} = \dfrac{12}{2.1875} = 5.49\,\text{A}\), i.e. about \(5.5\,\text{A}\).
Check by adding branch currents instead: \(\dfrac{12}{3} + \dfrac{12}{105/13} = 4 + 1.49 = 5.49\,\text{A}\).
Matches option A.

stem: Find the equivalent resistance
solution:
From the figure the \(10\,\Omega\) and \(15\,\Omega\) are in parallel between \(a\) and \(b\), then a \(5\,\Omega\) runs from \(b\) to \(d\); the lower path is a \(5\,\Omega\) and a \(6\,\Omega\) in series from \(a\) to \(d\).
\(10 \parallel 15 = \dfrac{10 \times 15}{25} = 6\,\Omega\).
Upper path \(= 6 + 5 = 11\,\Omega\).
Lower path \(= 5 + 6 = 11\,\Omega\).
The two paths are in parallel between the same terminals: \(R_{ad} = \dfrac{11 \times 11}{22} = 5.5\,\Omega\).
Matches option B.

stem: Two resistors are connected (a) in series (b) in parallel. The equivalent resistance in the two cases are 9 ohm and 2 ohm respectively. Then the resistances of the component resistors are
solution:
Given \(R_{1} + R_{2} = 9\) and \(\dfrac{R_{1}R_{2}}{R_{1}+R_{2}} = 2\), so \(R_{1}R_{2} = 2 \times 9 = 18\).
Two numbers with a known sum and product are the roots of \(x^{2} - 9x + 18 = 0\).
\((x-3)(x-6) = 0\), so the resistances are \(3\,\text{ohm}\) and \(6\,\text{ohm}\).
Check: \(3 + 6 = 9\) and \(\dfrac{3 \times 6}{9} = 2\).
Matches option B.

stem: Resistors of 1, 2 and 3 ohm are connected in the form of a triangle. If a 1.5 volt cell of negligible internal resistance is connected across 3 ohm resistor, the current flowing through this resistance will be
solution:
The cell is joined across the \(3\,\text{ohm}\) side of the triangle, so the \(1\,\text{ohm}\) and \(2\,\text{ohm}\) in series form the second path between the same two corners.
The cell has negligible internal resistance, so the full \(1.5\,\text{V}\) appears across the \(3\,\text{ohm}\) resistor.
\(I = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{1.5}{3}\).
\(= 0.5\,\text{amp}\).
The total current drawn from the cell is \(1\,\text{amp}\), since the other path also carries \(0.5\,\text{amp}\), but the question asks only for the part through this resistance.
Matches option B.

stem: Find the equivalent resistance if \(R_1 = 1\) ohm and \(R_2 = 2\) ohm
solution:
The figure is a ladder that repeats without end, so removing the first section leaves a network identical to the whole one.
If the equivalent resistance is \(R\), then \(R = R_{1} + \left(R_{2} \parallel R\right) = R_{1} + \dfrac{R_{2}R}{R_{2}+R}\).
\(R\left(R_{2}+R\right) = R_{1}\left(R_{2}+R\right) + R_{2}R\), so \(R^{2} - R_{1}R - R_{1}R_{2} = 0\).
Taking the positive root, \(R = \dfrac{R_{1} + \sqrt{R_{1}^{2} + 4R_{1}R_{2}}}{2}\).
With \(R_{1} = 1\) and \(R_{2} = 2\): \(R = \dfrac{1 + \sqrt{1+8}}{2} = \dfrac{1+3}{2} = 2\,\Omega\).
Check by truncating the ladder instead: one section gives \(3\,\Omega\), two give \(2.2\,\Omega\), three give \(2.048\,\Omega\), four give \(2.012\,\Omega\), settling on \(2\,\Omega\).
Matches option C.

stem: A copper wire of resistance R is cut into ten parts of equal length. Two pieces each are joined in series and then five such combinations are joined in parallel. The new combination will have a resistance
solution:
Cutting the wire into ten equal parts gives each piece a resistance \(\dfrac{R}{10}\).
Two joined in series: \(\dfrac{R}{10} + \dfrac{R}{10} = \dfrac{R}{5}\).
Five identical combinations in parallel divide that by five: \(\dfrac{1}{5} \times \dfrac{R}{5}\).
\(= \dfrac{R}{25}\).
Matches option D.

stem: n equal resistors are first connected in series and then connected in parallel. What is the ratio of the maximum to the minimum resistance
solution:
For \(n\) equal resistors of resistance \(R\), the series arrangement gives the maximum, \(R_{s} = nR\).
The parallel arrangement gives the minimum, \(R_{p} = \dfrac{R}{n}\).
\(\dfrac{R_{s}}{R_{p}} = \dfrac{nR}{R/n}\).
\(= n^{2}\).
Matches option C.

stem: Four resistances of \(100\,\Omega\) each are connected in the form of square. Then, the effective resistance along the diagonal points is
solution:
Between two diagonally opposite corners the square offers two paths, each made of two sides.
Each path: \(100 + 100 = 200\,\Omega\).
The two paths are in parallel: \(\dfrac{200 \times 200}{200+200} = \dfrac{40000}{400}\).
\(= 100\,\Omega\).
Matches option C.

stem: A wire has a resistance of 12 ohms. If it is bent in the form of a circle. The effective resistance between the two points on any diameter is equal to
solution:
The two ends of a diameter divide the ring into two equal halves.
Each half carries half the wire, so each is \(\dfrac{12}{2} = 6\,\Omega\).
The halves join the same two points, so they are in parallel: \(\dfrac{6 \times 6}{6+6}\).
\(= 3\,\Omega\).
Matches option B.

stem: Two copper wires of length l and 2l have radii, r and 2r respectively. What is the ratio of their specific resistances?
solution:
Specific resistance, or resistivity, is a property of the material alone.
It does not depend on the length or the radius of the specimen, which fix only the resistance \(R = \dfrac{\rho L}{A}\).
Both wires are copper, so both have the same \(\rho\) and the ratio is \(1:1\).
Matches option C.

stem: Two bulbs 25W, 220V and 100W, 220V are given. Which has higher resistance?
optC: both bulbs will have equal resistance
solution:
\(P = \dfrac{V^{2}}{R}\), so at a fixed rated voltage \(R = \dfrac{V^{2}}{P}\) and resistance varies inversely with the rated power.
\(R_{25} = \dfrac{220^{2}}{25} = 1936\,\Omega\).
\(R_{100} = \dfrac{220^{2}}{100} = 484\,\Omega\).
The lower-wattage bulb has the larger resistance, by a factor of four.
Matches option A.

stem: An electric heater of resistance \(6\,\Omega\) is run for 10 min on a 120 V line. The energy liberated in this period of time is
If a resistance coil is made by joining in parallel two resistances each of \(20\,\Omega\). An emf of 2V is applied across this coil for 100 seconds. The heat produced in the coil is
solution:
Two equal resistances in parallel halve the value: \(R = \dfrac{20}{2} = 10\,\Omega\).
\(H = \dfrac{V^{2}t}{R} = \dfrac{2^{2} \times 100}{10} = \dfrac{400}{10}\).
\(= 40\,\text{J}\).
Matches option C.

stem: Which of the following devices does NOT operate on the principle of the heating effect of electric current?
solution:
An electric iron warms its plate, a fuse melts, and a bulb glows, all because a current heats a resistive element - each is the heating effect.
A fan turns because a current-carrying coil experiences a torque in a magnetic field.
That is the magnetic effect of a current, not the heating effect.
Matches option D.

stem: A 220 V, 1000 W bulb is connected across a 110 V mains supply. The power consumed will be
solution:
From the rating, \(R = \dfrac{V^{2}}{P} = \dfrac{220^{2}}{1000} = 48.4\,\Omega\), taken as constant.
\(P' = \dfrac{V'^{2}}{R} = \dfrac{110^{2}}{48.4} = \dfrac{12100}{48.4}\).
\(= 250\,\text{W}\).
Equivalently, at constant resistance \(P \propto V^{2}\), so halving the voltage quarters the power: \(\dfrac{1000}{4} = 250\,\text{W}\).
Matches option D.
